which lockers remain open after all the students have toggled them. So, there are 100 lockers, all starting closed. Each student from 1 to 100 goes by and toggles certain lockers. Student 1 opens every locker, Student 2 toggles every second locker, and so on up to Student 100 who toggles just the 100th locker.

Hmm, the key here is to determine how many times each locker is toggled. Because each toggle changes the state of the locker—opening it if it's closed, closing it if it's open. So, if a locker is toggled an odd number of times, it will end up open; if even, closed.

Now, each locker number n is toggled by every student whose number is a divisor of n. For example, locker 6 is toggled by Student 1, 2, 3, and 6. So divisors of 6 are 1, 2, 3, 6. That means locker 6 is toggled 4 times, which is even, so it would end up closed.

Wait, right. So the number of times a locker is toggled is equal to the number of its divisors. So the problem reduces to finding which numbers between 1 and 100 have an odd number of divisors. Because only those lockers will be left open.

But normally, divisors come in pairs. For example, 6 has divisors 1 and 6, 2 and 3. So each divisor pairs with another. But if a number is a perfect square, like 16, one of its divisors is repeated. For 16, the divisors are 1, 2, 4, 8, 16. Wait, 4 is the square root of 16. So here, the divisor pairs are (1,16), (2,8), (4,4). So the square root is counted once, making the total number of divisors odd. Therefore, perfect squares have an odd number of divisors because one of the pairs is a repeated number.

So, lockers that are perfect squares will be toggled an odd number of times and thus remain open. All others will be toggled even times and end up closed.

Therefore, the lockers that remain open are those with numbers that are perfect squares. Let's list them: 1 (1²), 4 (2²), 9 (3²), 16 (4²), 25 (5²), 36 (6²), 49 (7²), 64 (8²), 81 (9²), 100 (10²). These are the squares of numbers from 1 to 10, since 10² is 100. So there are 10 lockers open at the end.
